content: Hugo Marie de Vries, born on February 16, 1848, in Haarlem, and deceased on May 21, 1935, in Lunteren, was a Dutch botanist and one of the pioneering figures in the field of genetics. He is primarily recognized for introducing the concept of genes, rediscovering Gregor Mendel's laws of heredity during the 1890s, and formulating a mutation theory of evolution. De Vries was the eldest son of Gerrit de Vries, a lawyer who later became a member of the Dutch Council of State in 1862, and Maria Everardina Reuvens, the daughter of an archaeology professor at Leiden University. His family moved to The Hague when his father assumed his council position. From a young age, Hugo exhibited a strong interest in botany, earning several awards for his herbarium collections while attending gymnasium in Haarlem and The Hague. In 1866, he enrolled at Leiden University to study botany, where he was particularly drawn to experimental botany as outlined in Julius Sachs' Lehrbuch der Botanik (1868). He was also deeply influenced by Charles Darwin's theory of evolution, despite his professor R. Suringar's skepticism. De Vries completed his dissertation on the effects of heat on plant roots, incorporating statements from Darwin to challenge his professor, and graduated in 1870. After a brief teaching stint, De Vries pursued further studies in chemistry and physics at Heidelberg University in September 1870, working in Wilhelm Hofmeister's laboratory. In the second semester, he joined Julius Sachs' laboratory in Würzburg to study plant growth. Between 1871 and 1875, he taught botany, zoology, and geology in Amsterdam schools, returning to Heidelberg during vacations to continue his research. In 1875, the Prussian Ministry of Agriculture offered him a professorship at the planned Royal Agricultural College in Berlin. In preparation, he moved back to Würzburg to study agricultural crops and collaborate with Sachs. However, by 1877, the Berlin College was still unbuilt, and De Vries briefly taught at the University of Halle-Wittenberg. That same year, he accepted a position as a lecturer in plant physiology at the newly established University of Amsterdam. He became an adjunct professor in 1878 and a full professor in 1881, partly to prevent him from moving to Berlin when the college finally opened. From 1885 to 1918, De Vries also served as professor and director of Amsterdam's Botanical Institute and Garden. In 1889, De Vries published Intracellular Pangenesis, where he proposed, based on a modified version of Darwin's 1868 pangenesis theory, that different traits are carried by distinct hereditary units. He referred to these units as pangenes, a term later shortened to genes by Wilhelm Johannsen. De Vries suggested that inheritance of specific traits in organisms occurs through these particles. To support his pangenesis theory, which initially received little attention, De Vries conducted hybridization experiments on plant varieties in the 1890s. He discovered new forms among wild evening primroses (Oenothera lamarckiana) and reached conclusions similar to Mendel's, confirming that inheritance of traits occurs in discrete particles. He speculated that genes could cross species barriers, with the same gene responsible for similar traits in different species. While this idea aligns with the concept of orthologous genes inherited from a common ancestor, De Vries envisioned physical gene transfer between species, a phenomenon that, while rare, does occur in higher organisms (e.g., horizontal gene transfer). In the late 1890s, De Vries became aware of Mendel's obscure paper from forty years earlier and adjusted some of his terminology accordingly. When he published his experimental results in the French journal Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences in 1900, he initially omitted mention of Mendel's work. However, after criticism from Carl Correns, he acknowledged Mendel's priority. Correns and Erich von Tschermak now share credit for rediscovering Mendel's laws. Interestingly, Correns had been a student of Nägeli, a botanist who corresponded with Mendel but failed to grasp the significance of his work, while Tschermak was the grandson of one of Mendel's botany teachers in Vienna. De Vries also developed a mutation theory of evolution, a form of saltationism, proposing that new species could arise in single, significant jumps rather than through Darwinian gradualism. However, it was later revealed that much of the evidence De Vries presented was unrelated to what is now understood as genetic mutation. Nonetheless, during his time, his theory was a leading contender for explaining evolution until the modern evolutionary synthesis emerged as the dominant model in the 1930s. In May 1905, De Vries was elected a Foreign Member of the Royal Society. He received the Darwin Medal in 1906 and the Linnean Medal in 1929. After retiring from the University of Amsterdam in 1918, he moved to his estate De Boeckhorst in Lunteren, where he maintained extensive experimental gardens. He continued his studies on new plant forms until his death in 1935.
